extracted.intended_audience: university technology transfer officers, university counsel, and technology commercialization professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Practical/legal guidance on copyright protection and related liabilities as applied to universities, university-created works (including software and databases), and service providers on the Internet. Covers statutory requirements, safe harbors (DMCA), ownership/transfer rules, defenses (fair use), and procedural/remedial rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: DMCA conduit safe harbor (§512(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: "a conduit for user content in a peer-to-peer network within the safe harbor defined in 512(a) and not subject to the notice and take down provision."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Service providers functioning as mere conduits may be covered by §512(a); subpoenas under §512(h) must identify the material to be removed or to which access is to be disabled. An ISP cannot remove or disable access to material stored on a user's computer. Cases suggest statutory amendment would be needed to extend subpoena power to transmission-without-modification safe harbor.

rubrics_metrics.name: DMCA subpoena identification requirement (§512(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: The subpoenas must identify the material to be removed or to which access is to be disabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For DMCA enforcement via subpoena, specificity as to the material/access to be disabled is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: ISP obligation to seek infringing information
rubrics_metrics.description: No obligation is imposed on ISPs to seek information indicating materials infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ISPs are not required proactively to monitor or investigate user content to discover infringement; different consequences attach if they receive notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: ISP direct vs contributory liability under DMCA
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability for direct infringement against a passive service provider is precluded by the legislative history of DMCA, but the ISP can be liable for contributory infringement after receiving actual or constructive notice under DMCA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receiving notice (actual or constructive) can expose an ISP to contributory liability even if passive; cases like Playboy v. Webbworld show operators who profit from infringing material may face liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicarious liability for profiting web operators
rubrics_metrics.description: Web site operators that sell infringing material and profit from the infringement (even in the form of a fixed monthly fee) can be liable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monetary benefit plus ability to control or supervise infringement can support vicarious liability (cited cases: Playboy Enterprises, et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-to-peer distribution and DMCA safe harbors
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer-to-peer distribution of copyrighted material does not meet the safe harbors available under DMCA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer-to-peer services have been held outside DMCA protections in multiple decisions (e.g., Napster litigation context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring by platforms may undermine DMCA immunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualified immunity under DMCA may be denied if monitoring results in a finding the operator knew and should have known of infringing material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A platform's proactive monitoring can create evidence it knew of infringing content; this has motivated some platforms (e.g., eBay) to change policies to monitor copyrighted material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat-infringer policy requirement for safe harbor eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to implement the required policy against repeat infringers (e.g., forwarding notices to an inactive e-mail address) may place a service provider outside DMCA safe harbor provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have denied safe-harbor protection where a provider failed to reasonably implement a repeat infringer policy (citing AOL decision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain services excluded from safe harbor (age-verification example)
rubrics_metrics.description: An adult Web site age-verification service was not within DMCA safe harbor provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particular business models or operational practices can disqualify a service from safe-harbor protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright exclusive rights and university ownership practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright grants certain exclusive rights to authors (or, in some cases, the author's employer). Universities have often granted faculty ownership of the copyright for 'scholarly works,' but works such as computer software and databases may not qualify for the scholarly-works exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ownership of copyrightable works at universities should be addressed in a written (and signed) policy; distinctions (e.g., scholarly works vs software/databases) should be explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for written university ownership/assignment policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Ownership must be addressed in a written (and signed) policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases illustrate universities enforcing policies to require assignment; clear written policies reduce dispute risk (e.g., graduate student and postdoc cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption of state-law rights by Copyright Act (17 U.S.C. §301)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Copyright Act preempts state law protection of rights equivalent to the exclusive rights of the copyright owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-law claims that require an extra element beyond copying may not be preempted; contract restrictions beyond copyrights can be enforceable (cases: ProCD, National Car Rental).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproduction/right implicated by transient copies and transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to reproduce is implicated when a work is stored in RAM, scanned, digitized, uploaded, downloaded, or transferred. Transmission by any device or process fixing a copy beyond the place from which it was sent (downloading and uploading) is treated as distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working Group on Intellectual Property Rights recommended clarification/amendment to address internet transmissions and importation by transmission as copyright infringement (citing MAI Systems / Peak Computer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter not protected (17 U.S.C. §102(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: No protection for ideas, plans, devices, or 'words and short phrases'; computer programs and databases have special considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held that names, short phrases, and purely functional elements are unprotectable; merger and scènes à faire doctrines also limit protection for elements dictated by efficiency or standard practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality requirement for compilations/databases (Feist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compilations/databases must meet the originality standard (Feist Publications v. Rural Telephone) — selection, coordination, or arrangement must possess a minimal degree of creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases show that originality can protect an arrangement; however, mere facts or standard listings (white pages) are not protected. Use of fictitious 'decoy' entries can be strong evidence of copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual protections (user agreements/shrinkwrap) against automated copying
rubrics_metrics.description: A user agreement prohibiting use of 'any robot, spider, or automatic device, or manual process to monitor or copy our web pages or the content contained herein' might provide protection under contract law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have enforced such contractual restrictions against automated scraping in various cases (e.g., eBay v. Bidder's Edge, Register.com v. Verio).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective work contributor limitation (17 U.S.C. §201(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: 17 U.S.C. 201(c) limits the copyright on a collective work to reproducing and distributing the contribution as part of the collective work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disputes arise over whether an electronic database constitutes the same collective work as a print compilation; rights of contributors are circumscribed for collective works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work-for-hire and historical-act differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Works created prior to January 1, 1978, are governed by the 1909 Act; work-for-hire analyses differ depending on applicable act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most material of commercial value is post-1977 and governed by the current Act, but older works and employee/commissioned works require attention to the applicable statutory regime and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signed writing required for exclusive transfer (17 U.S.C. §204(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A signed written transfer is necessary to establish an exclusive license; the writing must be executed more or less contemporaneously with the agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have enforced the writing requirement; lack of clear contract terms can lead to ownership disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration and formalities for remedies (17 U.S.C. §§408–412)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory provisions govern registration classes, deposits, and prerequisites for certain remedies; see 17 U.S.C. §§ 408(c), 410(c), 411, and 412.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration timing can affect availability of statutory damages and attorneys' fees; follow Copyright Office rules for classes (TX, PA, etc.) and deposit requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and criminal remedies (17 U.S.C. §504, §505; 18 U.S.C./2319)
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil remedies (e.g., §504 damages, §505 fees) and criminal penalties (e.g., 18 U.S.C. §2319(b)(1)) are available for infringement; remedies and potential restitution can be substantial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples show large civil and criminal exposures; compliance planning is important for institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-sale doctrine and importation limits (17 U.S.C. §109, §602)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first-sale doctrine allows certain resales; importation of copies not made in the U.S. may be prohibited by §602(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (Quality King, etc.) addresses resale and reimportation contexts; licenses may alter the 'sale' vs 'license' analysis (e.g., software EULAs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair use is fact-specific and multi-factorial
rubrics_metrics.description: Fair use analysis (17 U.S.C. §107) is fact-specific and considers transformative use, purpose, nature, amount, and effect on market; bad faith is not dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (Campbell, Sony, Princeton Univ. Press v. Michigan Document Services, etc.) shows varying outcomes depending on context (e.g., course packs, disassembly for interoperability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Merger and scènes à faire defenses limit protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Under merger and scènes à faire, elements dictated by efficiency or standard practice may be unprotectable; courts consider whether expression is 'indispensable' or 'standard' for a given idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software elements required for functional compatibility or efficiency may fall outside copyright protection (Altai, Apple cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied license criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: An implied license can exist only where an author creates a copyrighted work with knowledge and intent that the work would be used by another for a specific purpose; an implied license will not be implied based only on the unilateral expectations of one party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied-license findings often depend on contextual evidence (communications, dealing patterns); software cases include varying results on implied rights to modify or complete software.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence strategies for proving copying (decoys, selection/arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: In database contexts, inclusion of fictitious 'decoy' entries by an author can be strong evidence of copying when those decoys appear in a competitor's database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document preservation of unique/selective arrangements and decoys can be persuasive in proving copying; courts have issued injunctions for verbatim copying of database entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright management information (CMI) protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal or alteration of copyright management information can be actionable (discussed in circuitry examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases examine whether CMI was part of the original image and whether omission was intentional; practitioners should preserve and respect CMI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract terms can supplement copyright protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Contract terms beyond the scope of the copyright owner's exclusive rights can be enforceable (e.g., shrinkwrap, user agreements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of license terms to restrict scraping, redistribution, or commercial use can provide additional enforcement avenues under contract law (see ProCD, RealNetworks v. Streambox, Register.com v. Verio).
